meta.title: Danish B2 Upper Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Danish → English (see the Danish, recall the meaning) and English → Danish (see an English meaning, recall the Danish). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1500 words of Danish for an upper-intermediate learner, aligned to B2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main ideas of complex text on both concrete and abstract topics, including technical discussions in his/her field of specialisation' — a learner here is able to interact with a degree of fluency and spontaneity that makes regular interaction with native speakers quite possible without strain for either party, and to produce clear, detailed text on a wide range of subjects and explain a viewpoint on a topical issue giving the advantages and disadvantages of various options. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: Danish has examinations at these levels — Prøve i Dansk 1, 2 and 3 and Studieprøven — but none was found to publish a word list, so this deck is not an examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 147 of the 1500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — the economy and work, politics and the state, law and justice, science and technology, the environment and resources, health and society, media and communication, culture and society, the abstract nouns of discussion, the verbs of arguing and reasoning, describing and evaluating, and the connectors of formal Danish — and the other 1353 are the commonest remaining words of everyday Danish, taken from a frequency list built from film and television subtitles and counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. The 878 nouns are printed with their article — en or et — because the article is the gender, which decides the noun's definite ending, the adjective's ending and the pronoun that stands for it, and they show their definite singular and their plural (bilen, biler); the 318 verbs show their present, their past and their perfect with its auxiliary (spiser, spiste, har spist; går, gik, er gået), since Danish chooses between have and være by the verb, and behind the All forms fold their imperative, -s forms and participles. Real example sentences come with 1173 of the 1500 words, three apiece for 709 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.

We have not immortal souls, we shall never live again; like the green seaweed when once it has been cut off, we can never flourish more. Human beings, on the contrary, have souls which live forever, even after the body has been turned to dust. They rise up through the clear, pure air, beyond the glittering stars.
